cards.front: How are On-Demand Linux and Windows instances billed?
cards.back: **Per second with a 60-second minimum**, only while `running`. RHEL and Ubuntu Pro are also per second; SUSE Linux Enterprise Server is still billed per full hour.
cards.updated: RHEL and Ubuntu Pro now also billed per second (slides mention only Linux and Windows).

cards.front: Which purchasing option fits a short, unpredictable workload that must not be interrupted?
cards.back: **On-Demand**: no commitment, no upfront cost, highest hourly price.

cards.front: Which four instance attributes define a Reserved Instance's price (besides term, payment option and class)?
cards.back: **Instance type** (family + size), **Region**, **tenancy** (shared or dedicated) and **platform** (OS).

cards.front: Regional vs zonal Reserved Instance: which one reserves capacity?
cards.back: Only the **zonal** RI reserves capacity (in its AZ). A **regional** RI gives AZ flexibility and, for Linux/Unix default tenancy, size flexibility within the family, but no capacity.

cards.front: Standard vs Convertible RI: maximum discount and flexibility?
cards.back: **Standard**: up to 72% off; can be modified (AZ, scope, size) but never exchanged. **Convertible**: up to 66% off; can also be exchanged for another Convertible RI with a different family, OS, tenancy or scope in the same Region.

cards.front: What happens when a Reserved Instance's term ends?
cards.back: Nothing stops: matching instances keep running at **On-Demand rates**. RIs **do not auto-renew**; queue a new regional RI purchase to keep coverage.

cards.front: Which RIs can be sold in the Reserved Instance Marketplace?
cards.back: Only **Standard** RIs. Convertible RIs cannot be bought or sold there.

cards.front: What do you commit to with a Savings Plan, and what happens to usage above it?
cards.back: A **USD-per-hour spend** for 1 or 3 years. Usage above the hourly commitment is billed at **On-Demand** rates; unused commitment in an hour is still paid and does not carry over.

cards.front: EC2 Instance Savings Plan: what is it locked to, and what is flexible?
cards.back: Locked to **one instance family in one Region** (e.g. M7i in us-east-1). Flexible across **size, OS, tenancy and AZ**. Up to 72% off.

cards.front: What does a Compute Savings Plan cover?
cards.back: Any **EC2** usage regardless of family, size, Region, OS or tenancy, plus **Fargate** and **Lambda**. Up to 66% off.

cards.front: In what order are RIs and Savings Plans applied to an hour of EC2 usage?
cards.back: **Reserved Instances** first, then **EC2 Instance Savings Plans**, then **Compute Savings Plans**; whatever is left is billed **On-Demand**.

cards.front: Besides Compute and EC2 Instance, which other Savings Plan types exist?
cards.back: **SageMaker AI Savings Plans** (up to 64%) and **Database Savings Plans** (up to 35% on Aurora, RDS, DynamoDB, ElastiCache and other database services).
cards.updated: Database Savings Plans are newer than the slides.

cards.front: Spot Instances: maximum discount and warning before interruption?
cards.back: Up to **90%** off On-Demand, with a **two-minute interruption notice** (plus an earlier, optional rebalance recommendation signal).

cards.front: Should you set a maximum price for Spot Instances?
cards.back: Usually **no**. The recommended default is **No maximum price** (capped at the On-Demand price). A custom maximum causes more interruptions, and you always pay the current Spot price anyway.
cards.updated: Slides focus on a user-defined max price; AWS now recommends not setting one.

cards.front: What interruption behaviours can a Spot Instance have?
cards.back: **Terminate** (default), **stop** or **hibernate**. Stop and hibernate require a **persistent** request (or a `maintain` fleet) and keep the EBS data.

cards.front: Name good and bad workloads for Spot.
cards.back: **Good**: batch jobs, data analysis, image/video processing, CI builds, rendering, stateless containers behind a load balancer. **Bad**: databases, single critical servers, stateful work that cannot be stopped at short notice.

cards.front: One-time vs persistent Spot Instance request?
cards.back: **One-time**: closes once its instance is interrupted or terminated; nothing relaunches. **Persistent**: lives until cancelled or expired. After a stop or hibernate interruption EC2 restarts the same instance; if the instance is terminated, the request reopens and launches a new one.

cards.front: How do you permanently get rid of instances launched by a persistent Spot request?
cards.back: **Cancel the request first, then terminate the instances.** Terminating first makes the request launch a replacement; cancelling alone leaves running instances running.

cards.front: In which states can a Spot Instance request be cancelled?
cards.back: **open**, **active** or **disabled** (disabled = you stopped its instance). Cancelling a disabled request also terminates the stopped instance.

cards.front: What is a Spot Fleet, and what does AWS recommend instead today?
cards.back: A set of Spot Instances plus optional On-Demand Instances that works toward a target capacity across launch pools, within an optional max cost per hour. It is a **legacy API**; AWS recommends an **Auto Scaling group** or **EC2 Fleet**.
cards.updated: Spot Fleet is now described by AWS as legacy with no planned investment.

cards.front: Which Spot allocation strategy does AWS recommend for most workloads, and how does it work?
cards.back: **price-capacity-optimized** (`priceCapacityOptimized` in Spot Fleet): first picks the pools with the most spare capacity, then the cheapest of those.

cards.front: Why is the lowest-price Spot allocation strategy risky?
cards.back: It ignores capacity, so it has the **highest interruption risk**. AWS marks it not recommended, even though it is still the CLI default for fleets.

cards.front: When would you choose the diversified or capacity-optimized Spot strategy?
cards.back: **Diversified**: large, long-running fleets, so losing one pool affects only a fraction. **Capacity-optimized**: when interruptions are very costly (long CI, rendering, HPC).

cards.front: Which tenancy option lets you bring per-socket or per-core software licences (BYOL)?
cards.back: A **Dedicated Host**: a whole physical server with visible sockets and cores, host affinity and placement control. Billed per host; reservations up to 70% off.

cards.front: What are Dedicated Instances, and what extra fee do they carry?
cards.back: Instances on hardware dedicated to **your account** (may share with your own other instances), with no placement control. Billed per instance plus **USD 2/hour per Region** where any Dedicated Instance runs.

cards.front: How is an On-Demand Capacity Reservation billed?
cards.back: At the **On-Demand rate whether or not instances use it**. No term for immediate-use reservations; cancel any time. A matching running instance is billed instead of the reservation, not on top of it.

cards.front: Which discounts can apply to a Capacity Reservation?
cards.back: **Regional Reserved Instances** and **Savings Plans**. Zonal RI discounts do **not** apply to Capacity Reservations.

cards.front: Which three things actually reserve EC2 capacity?
cards.back: A **zonal RI**, an **On-Demand Capacity Reservation** (or Capacity Block for ML) and an allocated **Dedicated Host**. Regional RIs and Savings Plans are discounts only.

cards.front: What are Capacity Blocks for ML?
cards.back: Reservations of **accelerated ML instances** (P-family GPUs and Trainium) for a set period starting up to **eight weeks** ahead, placed in EC2 UltraClusters. They cannot be cancelled.
cards.updated: Not in the slides; added as a newer capacity option.
